title: Hooke's law and Young's modulus: comparing steel, copper and aluminium
examples: Why is steel stiffer than aluminium?
How do I calculate the extension of a bar?

curves.label: Aluminium, E = 69 GPa
curves.ask: How do I calculate the extension of a bar?

explain.say: In 1678 Robert Hooke wrote that the stretch of a spring is in proportion to the force. The same holds for a steel bar, as long as you stay in the elastic range. Divide stress by strain and you get a number that belongs to the material, not to the bar: Young's modulus, E. Look at the three straight lines.

explain.say: Each line is a material, and its slope is E. Steel has the steepest slope: 200 gigapascals. That means a stress of 100 megapascals stretches steel by only 0.0005, half a thousandth. See the steep line reach 100 at the dashed mark? Which material stretches most for the same stress?

explain.say: Aluminium, with the gentlest slope: E is about 69 gigapascals, roughly a third of steel. Take a 3 metre bar at 100 megapascals. Steel stretches by 1.5 millimetres, aluminium by about 4.35 millimetres, nearly three times as much. Can you work out copper's stretch?

explain.say: About 2.6 millimetres. Now zoom out to see how wide the range is. Rubber is about 0.05 gigapascals, wood along the grain about 11, and diamond over 1000. See the bars, with rubber too small to notice? Notice E measures stiffness, not strength. Is a stiff material always strong?

draw.text: Stiffness (E) and strength (yield stress) are different

explain.say: No! Glass is stiff but cracks easily. Excellent work! Real link: aircraft use aluminium because stiffness per kilogram is what counts, and its low density makes up for its lower E. Exam tip: Young's modulus barely changes with heat treatment or alloying, but strength changes a lot. Challenge: what stress stretches steel by 0.1 percent?

draw.text: Same E for most steels, from cheap rebar to springs

faq.a: It is the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic range: E equals sigma over epsilon. It measures how stiff a material is, and is the slope of the straight part of the stress-strain curve.

faq.q: Why is steel stiffer than aluminium?
faq.a: Its atoms are held by stronger, more tightly packed bonds, so it takes more stress to pull them apart by the same strain. Steel's E is about 200 gigapascals, aluminium's about 69.

faq.q: How do I calculate the extension of a bar?
faq.a: Use delta equals F L over A E, or sigma times L over E. Keep units consistent, for example newtons, millimetres and megapascals.

faq.q: What is the difference between stiffness and strength?
faq.a: Stiffness, measured by E, is how much a material resists stretching. Strength is how much stress it can take before yielding or breaking. A material can be stiff but weak, like glass.

faq.q: When does Hooke's law stop working?
faq.a: It holds only in the elastic, straight-line part of the curve. Beyond the limit of proportionality, stress is no longer proportional to strain.

facts: Young's modulus of steel is about 200 gigapascals; of aluminium, about 69 gigapascals.
The extension of a bar under axial load is F L divided by A E.

quiz.say: A 2 metre steel rod is stressed to 150 megapascals. E is 200 gigapascals. How much does it stretch?
quiz.show: 2 m steel rod at 150 MPa, E = 200 GPa. Extension?

wrong.1: That uses a length of 1 metre instead of 2.
wrong.2: That is ten times too big; check the gigapascal to megapascal conversion.

quiz.say: Two bars of the same size carry the same load. Bar A has twice the Young's modulus of bar B. Bar A stretches…
quiz.show: Same size and load; bar A has twice the E of bar B. Bar A stretches…
quiz.why: Extension is F L over A E, so doubling E halves the stretch.

wrong.1: A higher modulus means stiffer, so less stretch.
wrong.2: The stretch depends on E, so it cannot be the same.
